prize_parts.citation: for theories of firm heterogeneity and selection that transformed the analysis of international trade, exporting and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extensions moved trade theory from the representative firm to selection, reallocation and the extensive margin. This yielded sharp, testable predictions about exporter premia, within-industry reallocation and welfare gains, and firm-level data have confirmed much of this over more than twenty years. The framework is now standard across trade, macro and development. It is conceptually distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize on new trade theory. Of the leading candidates it has the cleanest credit assignment, because Melitz is the clear originator and Helpman is the natural second laureate through the joint exporter-versus-FDI work and his earlier trade theory. The opening rankings give it the broadest support in the top three (nine of ten ranked it there), including from members outside trade and from members who ranked other candidates first. I ranked B049 first in my opening. After weighing colleagues' arguments I now put B048 first, because B049 and B001 have attribution or identification problems that B048 does not have to the same degree.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the empirical origins of firm-level trade facts are shared with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on this ballot entry, so a Melitz-Helpman prize may be criticised as leaving out part of the discovery. Some welfare implications also depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity. Trade was also recognised in 2008, so the field balance could count against it, though that is not a scientific argument.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B048 third and would add Stephen Redding to Melitz and Helpman for the quantitative trade and spatial extensions.
responses.response: I agree Redding's quantitative and spatial work is important, but it is a later wave that builds on, and is not constitutive of, the selection mechanism. Adding him dilutes a clean two-name credit and invites a second question about Bernard, Eaton and Kortum, who are not on this ballot. I keep the two-name configuration and treat the quantitative-trade extension as a separate achievement that the committee could consider later.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B001 first and B049 second, and he would credit only Persson and Tabellini in B049, treating Besley as secondary to the constitutions and fiscal-policy core.
responses.response: I share the view that the Besley strand on state capacity and accountability is a distinct programme, and this is why I now hesitate over B049. A prize built on Persson and Tabellini alone is defensible, but it then rests on cross-country constitutional identification that Strömberg himself and others call contested. I keep B049 as my first alternative, but I think the B048 case is more robust on both credit and evidence.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B001 first for its combination of new cross-country data and explanatory structure, but flags that the legal-origins thesis has been criticised on causal identification and that excluding Vishny is a real attribution cost.
responses.response: I agree B001 is among the most influential bodies of work and I ranked it second. But the points she raises weigh against placing it first. The headline causal claim is the contested part, and the three-name cap excludes a co-author of the core papers. B048 has also been tested in firm-level data and its core predictions have held up reasonably well. B001 stays as my second alternative because its influence on research is very large.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B015 first and B048 second. He calls the heterogeneous-firm work arguably the most important trade advance since 2008, and he notes that a thematic overlap with the 2024 institutions prize and a possible conflict over Persson could affect B049.
responses.response: I agree with his assessment of B048. His point about B049 matters to me: thematic overlap with the 2024 prize, together with the proximity of some members to Persson, makes B049 harder to defend on the merits alone. I do not share his first-place view of B015. The China-shock magnitudes and persistence are still debated, the work is more recent, and Dorn's exclusion by the three-name cap and the task-model lineage outside the ballot complicate attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would want Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum or Yeaple credited alongside Melitz and Helpman, which the ballot entry does not allow.
Whether Helpman's credit in B048 interacts with his separate appearance in the trade-politics candidate, as noted by colleagues.
How sensitive the estimated welfare gains from selection are to functional-form assumptions.
Whether I am underweighting the case for B049 or B001, given my own earlier first and second rankings and the strong first-place support for B001.
My assessments rely on prior knowledge of the literature and are not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Melitz, Helpman, Redding, Persson, Tabellini, Besley, Shleifer, La Porta or Lopez-de-Silanes. My general field is microeconomic theory and market design, which is not the field of the candidate I propose. The profile mentions SSE affiliation with several committee members, which is not a candidate connection.
